The European edible sea urchin Echinus esculentus begins life as a fertilised egg, from which a planktotrophic bipinnaria larva develops. Upon hatching, the newly formed embryo carries a minute wet weight of just 0.00000088 grams [Wwb = 0.00000088 grams]. This minuscule mass, comparable to values recorded in the heart urchin Echinocardium cordatum, underscores the substantial energetic challenge faced during the free-swimming larval phase. The bipinnaria larva drifts and feeds within the plankton, undergoing a transformation into the characteristic pluteus larva as it grows. During this protracted planktonic period, the larva must accumulate sufficient resources to reach metamorphic competence and settle onto the substratum.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the time since birth at metam, encompassing the entire planktonic phase, has been recorded as 45 days since birth . This developmental interval is critical, as it determines the duration of vulnerability to pelagic predators. At the point of metamorphosis, the larva measures approximately 0.09 centimeters  in length, a value that aligns closely with the size range of 0.68 to 0.95 millimeters reported for related echinoid species. The successful completion of metamorphic climax and settlement marks the transition from a bilateral larval body plan to the radial symmetry of the post-metamorphic juvenile.

Once settled, the juvenile sea urchin enters a phase of rapid linear growth in test diameter. Field records indicate that the test diameter at puberty, representing the size at which gonadal maturation begins, is 6.1 centimeters [Lp = 6.1 centimeters]. Reaching this size milestone typically requires an extended period of growth. Available data suggest that the time since birth at puberty is 730 days since birth [tp = 730 days since birth] for individuals reared at a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], placing the onset of reproductive maturity at approximately two years of age. This timing appears to be broadly consistent across populations in the North Atlantic, although local thermal conditions may modulate the exact schedule. The corresponding wet weight at puberty for a sea urchin of this diameter is approximately 96 grams [Wwp = approximately 96 grams].

As individuals continue to grow beyond the pubertal threshold, their body dimensions increase steadily. The ultimate test diameter recorded for Echinus esculentus is 17.6 centimeters [Li = 17.6 centimeters], a size that represents the maximum horizontal span of the calcareous test in fully grown adults. This large test diameter corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 2312 grams [Wwi = 2312 grams], positioning this species among the heavier regular echinoids inhabiting the northeastern Atlantic. The maximum recorded longevity in wild populations has been estimated at approximately 16 years [am = approximately 16 years] when assessed at a stable environmental temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], indicating that individuals can live for approximately sixteen years under favorable conditions.

Reproductive effort in this species is intense and linked to thermal regime. When water temperatures reach 15 °C [T = 15 °C], spawning females can release extraordinarily high numbers of oocytes in a single spawning event, with a maximum reproductive output of approximately 20 million oocytes per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 20 million oocytes per spawning event]. This spawning event occurs once per year [F_R_i = event occurs once per year], yielding a high annual fecundity that is characteristic of echinoids with planktotrophic larvae. The combination of a large adult body size and a high fecundity schedule suggests that Echinus esculentus adopts a strategy of producing numerous offspring to compensate for the high mortality rates characteristic of its prolonged pelagic larval stage.
